In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

.

Commentary on Surah al-Muzzammil

It is Meccan.

According to some, it is Meccan except for the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾, up to the end of the surah.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who wraps himself up﴾ mean: O you who wraps himself up (al-mutazzammil). The tā' was assimilated into the zāy. Similarly, the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who covers himself﴾ mean: O you who covers himself (al-mutaddaththir). The tā' was assimilated into the dāl.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When Jibril, upon him be blessings from Allah, appeared to him at the beginning of the revelation, he was seized by intense fear, so he returned to his household and wrapped himself in his garments. Then Allah, the Exalted, sent down His words: ﴿O you who wraps himself up﴾. Then Jibril, upon him be peace, came to him frequently until he became at ease.

Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi said: He was wrapped in a qaṭīfa (a thick woolen cloak).

It is related from al-Ḍaḥḥak regarding His words: ﴿O you who wraps himself up﴾, that it means: O you who sleeps.

In some reports, Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him while he was sleeping and said: "O you who wraps himself up," i.e., the sleeper, "arise, and take for yourself a shade on a day when there is no shade but His shade."

In some tafsirs, it is related from ʿIkrima: ﴿O you who wraps himself up﴾ means: O you who is wrapped in prophethood.

This is a strange (gharīb) interpretation.

And [a verse] is recited regarding al-muzzammil:

(As if Thabir, among the ʿarānīn of Wabila, were a noble man of the Anas tribe, wrapped in a coarse cloak.)

And it is recited in the irregular (shādhdh) reading: "O you who wraps himself up" (al-muzzammil).

And His saying: ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little﴾, i.e., except a small portion of it.

Al-Kalbi said: it is a third [of the night]; its meaning is: stand [in prayer] for two-thirds of the night.

And from Wahb ibn Munabbih: "except a little" is less than a sixth.

And His saying, ﴿half of it﴾ indicates the night, meaning: stand [in prayer] for half of it, except a little.

It has also been said, regarding the "little" in this view, that it is a sixth (al-sudus) of the night.

And His saying, ﴿or reduce it a little﴾ means: from the half down to a third.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 4:

And His words ﴿or add to it﴾ mean: add to the half up to two-thirds.

The meaning of the verse is: an obligation to stand [in prayer] during it, with a broadening of the amount.

Al-Naqqash mentioned that His words "half of it" mean: or half of it.

And His words ﴿and recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾ mean: explain it with clear explanation.

Al-Dahhak said: letter by letter.

The reality of tartil (measured recitation, deliberate chanting) is deliberateness in recitation and giving each letter its due of elongation, without haste and without (hadhramah) [rapid, slurred gabbling].

Abu Jamrah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "That I recite Surah al-Baqarah in measured recitation is more beloved to me than that I recite the whole Qur'an in (hadhramah)."

And from Anas, that he was asked about the recitation of the Prophet, and he said: "He used to elongate (the vowels) with extension."

In the narrations (al-hikayat) it is related from Sadaqah al-Maqabiri that he said: "I stood one night and recited quickly (ahdar hadran), and I saw in a dream as if I were sowing barley. Then I recited with tartil, and I saw in a dream as if I were sowing wheat. Then I recited with precision (tahqiq), and I saw in a dream as if I were sowing sesame."

It is also authentically transmitted through the narration of Sa'd ibn Hisham that he said: "I said to 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: Inform me about the Messenger of Allah's night prayer."

She said: "Do you not recite Surah al-Muzzammil?" I said: "Yes."

She said: "Allah the Exalted made the night prayer obligatory upon the Prophet and his Companions, and they stood for a year until their feet swelled. Then Allah the Exalted sent down His words: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾, and the night prayer was abrogated."

In this report it is stated that the beginning of the surah was revealed and its final part was withheld for a year.

In some narrations: sixteen months.

In some strange narrations: ten years.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 5:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We will cast upon you a heavy word﴾. Al-Hasan said: "Heavy" means that acting upon it is difficult.

Al-Zajjaj said: It refers to the prayer, the fasting, and the rest of the commands and prohibitions, which a person does not perform except with an effort that weighs heavily upon him.

It is related from Qatadah that he said: By Allah, its limits and its obligations are heavy.

It has also been said: "Heavy" means heavy in the Scale on the Day of Resurrection; this was said by al-Hasan in one of the two narrations.

Al-Farra' said: "A heavy word" means it is not light and not worthless, and it is heavy, that is, it has weight through its soundness, its clarity, and its firmness.

It is said: "This is a sound, weighty speech (kalam razin sin)," meaning: it is not a statement that has no meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 6:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the rising at night﴾. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that it refers to the entire night.

And from Ibn 'Umar and Anas: it is what lies between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

And from al-Kisa'i: the beginning of the night.

And from some of them: from the last 'Isha' prayer until Subh. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba.

And from Ibn al-A'rabi: it is that one awakens after having slept.

And nashi'at al-layl (the rising at night): the hours of the night. Its real meaning is that the hours of nashi'a are of the night, i.e., those in which some of them arise one after another.

And His words: ﴿it is stronger in tread﴾. It was also read as "wiṭa'" (وطاء). As for His words ﴿wat'an﴾, al-Akhfash Sa'id ibn Mas'ada said: "stronger in standing."

And wat' (الْوَطْء, treading/trampling) in the language is heaviness.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Press down hard upon Mudar" (اشْدُد وطأتك على مُضر).

It is said: "The authority of the ruler (sultan) became severe in such-and-such a land," i.e., its heaviness.

Based on this, the meaning of His words ﴿stronger in tread﴾ is: heavier.

The meaning is that it is heavier upon the body, because it is the time of rest and stillness, so standing in it is heavier. And when standing is heavier, the reward is greater, for when the exertion is greater and the labour more tiring, the reward is greater. This is what is meant by the verse in this reading.

As for the second reading, namely ﴿ashaddu mu'ata'atan﴾ (أشد مواطأة), its meaning is agreement between hearing, sight and heart, and that is because of the fewness of movements and the stillness of sounds. For during the day the eye is occupied with looking, the ear with hearing, and the heart is occupied with its affairs, so there is no agreement in listening and understanding.

al-Farra' said: ﴿stronger in tread﴾ means more fitting that you may count the measures of your standing, due to the emptiness of your hearts.

And His words ﴿and more upright in speech﴾: al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: clearer in speech.

And it is narrated from Anas that he read His words ﴿stronger in tread﴾ as "ahya' wat'an" (أهيأ وطاء), and this is close in meaning to the first.

And it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Nashi'at al-layl is the whole of the night in Abyssinian (Habashi)," and it is an arabized word (mu'arraba).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 73, verse 7:

The words of God Most High: ﴿Indeed, for you by day there is extended occupation﴾ mean: extended free time for rest.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "Sabhan tawilan" means: movement, coming and going, in your affairs.

Yahya ibn Ya'mar recited "sabkhan tawilan" with the letter khā' (with a dot), i.e. "sabkhan."

Tha'lab said: al-sabḥ (sabḥ, with ḥā') is agitation and restlessness, and al-sabkh (sabkh, with khā') is stillness.

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) concerning the thief of her property: "Do not be lenient (lā tastabkhī) in your opinion regarding him," meaning: do not lighten (your judgment).

And [the words of God]: ﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾. Muqatil said: when you recite, say: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" at the beginning of the surah.

It is also said: mention your Lord.

And His words: ﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾, meaning: cut yourself off to Him with complete cutting off (inqita').

From this comes "al-'adhra' al-batul" (the virgin) for Maryam, meaning: one who has cut herself off to Allah, the Exalted, in worship (nusk).

Likewise "al-Zahra' al-Batul" for Fatimah, meaning: one who was cut off from her peers in excellence. From this also comes "sadaqah batlah," meaning a charity that is severed and removed from the property of the one who gives it.

It is also said: ﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾ means: be sincere to Him with complete sincerity.

Al-Naqqash related from Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir that he raised his hands in prayer.

And from Zayd ibn Aslam that he renounced the world and sought what is with Allah, the Exalted.

The Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but Him, so take Him as a trustee (wakīl).

Al-Farrā' said: "a guarantor (kafīl)."

It is said: "a god (ilāhan)."

It is said: "all your affairs."

God's words, "And be patient over what they say" (﴿واصبر على ما يقولون﴾), refer to the beginning of Islam, before the revelation of the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf). Likewise His words, "and part from them with a graceful parting" (﴿واهجرهم هجرا جميلا﴾), have been abrogated (nusikha) by the verse of the sword.

The "graceful parting" (al-hajr al-jamīl) is said to be that in which there is no impatience or complaint (jaza').

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 11:

The words of His, the Exalted: ﴿Leave Me with those who deny, [who are] possessors of luxury﴾. If someone asks: what is the meaning of His words ﴿Leave Me with those who deny﴾ when there is no barrier separating them from Him?

The answer: the Arabs say this even when there is no barrier or obstacle, as we have explained.

His words ﴿possessors of luxury﴾ mean: those given to indulgence (al-tana'um).

In some reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) it is said: "Indeed, the servants of Allah are not those given to indulgence."

His words "and give them respite for a little" mean: I will grant them a respite of a short duration.

ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: There was not between the revelation of this verse and the battle of Badr except a little (yasir).

It has also been said that the verse was revealed concerning the sons of al-Mughira, namely al-Mughira ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar ibn Makhzum.

It is also said that it was revealed concerning twelve men of Quraysh, who were the feeders (al-mut'imun) on the day of Badr.

Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles﴾, meaning: fetters.

Al-Khansa' said:

(He called you, so she cut off his shackles... and had you not been there, O Sakhr, she would not have cut them.)

Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: ﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles﴾ means: bridles of fire.

As for His saying: ﴿and a blazing fire﴾, we have already explained it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 13:

And His saying: ﴿And a food that chokes⦈. Mujahid said: it is the zaqqum. It has also been said: it is a thorn that lodges in the throat, so it neither goes down nor comes out.

It has also been said: it is the dari' (a thorny, bitter plant).

It is related in accounts that al-Hasan al-Basri fasted for three nights without breaking his fast, and whenever food was brought to him he would recite this verse and order it removed, until he was afterwards compelled to drink a bowl of sawiq (a porridge of ground grain).

And there has come in some strange reports that the Prophet (ﷺ) had this verse recited in his presence, and he fell into a swoon. This is very strange.

His saying: ﴿and a painful punishment⦈: that is, painful (causing pain).

In some reports it is said that Allah, exalted is He, loves the nakl upon the nakl.

That is: the strong, experienced man upon the experienced horse.

Almost all of the passage is commentary on Qur'an 73:14, so I'll translate it in full.

Allah the Exalted's words: ﴿On the Day when the earth and the mountains quake﴾ means: they are shaken violently, and from this comes "ar-rajfah" (the quaking), i.e., the earthquake.

And His words: ﴿and the mountains will become heaps of sand, flowing﴾ mean: sand that is flowing.

It is said: "al-muhayyal" (the loose, shifting sand-heap) is that which, when one side of it is taken, the other side collapses and pours down.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 15:

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger, a witness over you﴾ refers to Muhammad.

And His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ refers to Musa (Moses), may the blessings of Allah be upon him.

And His saying: ﴿So Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger﴾, meaning: he departed from His command.

And His saying: ﴿So We seized him with a severe seizure﴾, meaning: harsh.

It is said: "A wabil food" when a person eats it and it does not agree with him (lit. he does not digest it).

And it has been said: wabilan means heavy.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How, then, will you guard yourselves, if you disbelieve, against a Day that will turn children gray-haired?﴾ That is: how will you guard yourselves [if you disbelieve] from the punishment of a Day? Then He described the Day, saying: ﴿that will turn children gray-haired.﴾ This is in the manner of the Arabs' speech when mentioning the severity of a day. They say: "It is a day when foreheads turn gray (tashīb al-nawāṣī)," and "a day when the pitch (al-qār) turns white."

So the purpose of the verse is to inform about the severity of the matter.

It is also said in tafsir that the children who turn gray-haired on that Day are the children of the disbelievers, not the children of the believers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 18:

As for His saying: ﴿the heaven will be split asunder by it﴾, it has been related from many of the early scholars (al-salaf) that His saying ﴿split asunder by it﴾ means "by Allah," and this is the descent (nuzul) on the Day of Resurrection to decide the judgment, without asking how (bila kayf).

It has also been said: "the heaven will be split asunder by it" means "in it," meaning that the heaven will be cleaved on the Day of Resurrection.

This was mentioned by Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas, who said that it is the best of the meanings.

As for His saying: ﴿His promise is ever fulfilled﴾, it means: certain to occur, undoubtedly taking place.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 19:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ — meaning: the surah is a reminder, a lesson, and an admonition.

His words: ﴿So whoever wills may take to his Lord a way﴾ — meaning: a path and a direction toward Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 73, verse 20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it﴾. It is also recited as "wa-nisfahu" (and half of it). Whoever reads it with a fatha on the fa' (nisfahu, as "nisfah") makes it accusative as an explanation of "adna" (less). Whoever reads it with a kasra on the fa' means: "adna min nisfihi" (less than half of it).

His saying, ﴿and a third of it﴾, is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "half" in both readings.

His saying, ﴿and a group of those with you﴾: we have already explained that the Prophet and his Companions stood [in prayer] for a year, until their feet swelled.

It is related in tafsir that they used to stand the whole night, out of fear that they might fall short of the prescribed amount.

There is a difference of opinion as to whether standing in prayer at night was obligatory upon the Prophet and all his Companions, or upon the Prophet alone.

In one of the two opinions, it was obligatory upon him and upon all his Companions.

In another opinion, it was obligatory upon him alone. This was mentioned by Abu al-Hasan al-Mawardi, who also mentioned two opinions as to whether the night standing remained incumbent upon him after abrogation (naskh): ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, and a group of those with you. And Allah measures the night and the day. He knows that you could not keep count of it, so He has turned to you in forgiveness. So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾.

As for the first of the two opinions: the abrogation applied to the Companions, while for the Prophet it remained until Allah took him (in death).

The second opinion: it became abrogated for him and for the Companions all together, and only voluntary supererogatory prayer (tatawwu') at night remained.

His saying, ﴿And Allah measures the night and the day﴾, means: the hours of the night and the day are not hidden from His knowledge, so He knows what they stand [in prayer] of it and what they leave.

His saying, ﴿He knows that you could not keep count of it﴾, means: you could not [bear it].

The meaning is: it is difficult for you to determine the prescribed amount and to fulfil the command, because a person who sleeps and then wakes up does not know how long he slept and how much of the night remains. Allah had prescribed night standing for a known amount, which would not fall below a third, and could reach two-thirds if one wished.

His saying, ﴿so He has turned to you﴾, means: He abrogated it for you and relinquished it. The meaning of tawbah here is removal and pardon.

His saying, ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ has two interpretations:

One: pray what is easy of (the prayer), and this is by way of supererogatory and voluntary prayer, not by way of obligation.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: night standing is obligatory, even if one were to milk a sheep, due to this verse. The more correct is the first opinion, "because it is established that a Bedouin came to the Prophet with disheveled head, his voice resounding, and not understanding what he said... the report until he said: Is there anything else incumbent upon me? He said: No, except that you perform voluntary prayer." (The Prophet's answer concerned the five prayers.) ... [the verse continues:] ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others who fight in the way of Allah﴾.

This report indicates that night standing is not obligatory, and there is consensus on this.

The second opinion: His saying, ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ means: recite in the prayer what is easy of the Qur'an, without restriction or prescribed measure.

This is the view of al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars regarding what follows al-Fatihah.

Abu al-Hasan al-Daraqutni mentioned in his book, with his chain of transmission from Qays ibn Abi Hazim, who said: I prayed behind Ibn 'Abbas, and he recited al-Fatihah in the first rak'ah and the first verse of Surat al-Baqarah. Then he stood for the second rak'ah and recited al-Fatihah and the second verse of Surat al-Baqarah. When he finished, he recited the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾, meaning: that which is easy.

Ali ibn Umar, who is al-Daraqutni, said: this is evidence for the view of those who say that what is easy is what comes after al-Fatihah.

His saying, ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill﴾, means: those afflicted with illness.

His saying, ﴿and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾, means: merchants and all other travellers.

His saying, ﴿and others who fight in the way of Allah﴾, means: those who go out to fight.

All of these explain the forms of hardship involved in night standing.

His saying, ﴿So recite of it what is easy﴾, its meaning is as we have explained.

His saying, ﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾, means: the five obligatory prayers and the obligatory zakah.

It is said that zakah here means zakat al-ru'us (zakah on heads), which is zakat al-fitr.

It is said: ﴿And lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾, which we have mentioned before.

It is said: it is all the supererogatory prayers and the various forms of prayer.

It is said: it is the saying "Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, and Allahu akbar."

It is said: it is spending on one's family.

His saying, ﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾, means: its reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, ﴿better and greater in reward﴾: it is in the accusative as the second object of "tajiduhu" (you will find it).

It is said: it is a separating expression (fasl al-kalam), mentioned by al-Azhari.

His saying, ﴿and greater in reward﴾ is conjoined to the first.

His saying, ﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah; indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: its meaning is apparent. And Allah knows best.
